# What an easier benchmark would have let us claim

*Generated by `scripts/compare_ablations.py`. Every row is the identical pipeline and the identical
model, run over 60 synthetic patients under a different set of simulation assumptions. Nothing about
the twin changes between rows — only how hard the test is.*

## Why this file exists

A digital twin validated against a simulator built from the twin's own equations measures parameter
error, not the thing that breaks twins in clinic: the body doing something the model has no term for.
Add a meal schedule the model already knows and the prediction task quietly becomes a timetable
lookup. Both shortcuts are common, and both inflate results substantially. This table is how much.

> **Read AUPRC across rows with care.** Making the simulation easier also changes how often events
> happen — the hypoglycaemia base rate varies about two-fold across these settings — and AUPRC moves
> with prevalence. The prevalence-adjusted **lift** (AUPRC ÷ base rate) and the **forecast RMSE** are
> the columns that compare like with like.

| Setting | Body model | Eating | plan↔reality carb r | Hypo base rate | Hypo AUPRC | Hypo lift | Hyper lift | Twin RMSE @120 min |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Hard (as submitted)** | **different** | **messy** | 0.56 | 1.15% | 0.135 | 11.8× | 8.5× | 38 mg/dL |
| Matched model | same as twin | **messy** | 0.56 | 0.61% | 0.291 | 47.3× | 6.4× | 37 mg/dL |
| Easy meals | **different** | near-oracle | 0.81 | 1.17% | 0.176 | 15.1× | 12.3× | 29 mg/dL |
| Matched + easy | same as twin | near-oracle | 0.81 | 0.53% | 0.061 | 11.6× | 8.9× | 23 mg/dL |

## What each shortcut is worth

**Forecast error is the cleanest comparison**, because it does not depend on how often events happen.
Taking both shortcuts moves the twin's 2-hour RMSE from **38 mg/dL to 23 mg/dL** — a 40% reduction bought entirely by making the simulation kinder.

The two shortcuts are not equal. Predictable eating alone takes RMSE to **29 mg/dL**; removing model misspecification alone barely moves it (**37 mg/dL**). For a 2-hour horizon, knowing what the patient is about to eat matters more than having the right equations.

A 2-hour glucose forecast error of 23 mg/dL would sit well ahead of the published state of the art, which is roughly 30–40 mg/dL on real CGM data. That is the tell: when a simulation study reports forecast errors far below what anyone achieves in the clinic, the simulator is usually the reason.

**On discrimination, model misspecification is the expensive one.** Letting the body run the twin's own equations lifts hypoglycaemia detection from **12× the base rate to 47×** — the twin suddenly knows the patient exactly, because the patient was built from its own assumptions.

### Caveats on this table

* These are 60-patient runs, so the rarest cell (hypoglycaemia under the easiest settings) rests on very few events and its lift estimate is unstable. Directions are meaningful; third decimals are not.
* Making the simulation easier changes event rates as well as predictability, which is exactly why prevalence is printed beside AUPRC rather than left implicit.

We report the hard numbers in the README and keep this file so the difference is auditable.

## Reproducing this table

```bash
make ablations                      # runs all four settings
python scripts/compare_ablations.py  # regenerates this file
```

Each run writes its own `reports/metrics_*.json`, so every number above can be traced to a file.
